Work Done by a Force: Work is done when a force moves an object through a displacement. For a constant force, W = F d cos(theta), where theta is the angle between the force and the displacement. Work is a scalar measured in joules (1 J = 1 N m). It is positive when the force has a component along the motion, zero when the force is perpendicular to the motion or there is no displacement, and negative when the force opposes the motion, as friction does. The area under a force versus displacement graph equals the work. Net work is the sum of the work done by all forces.
Kinetic Energy and the Work-Energy Theor: Kinetic energy is the energy of motion, KE = 1/2 m v^2, measured in joules. It depends on the square of the speed, so doubling the speed quadruples the kinetic energy. The work-energy theorem says the net work done on an object equals its change in kinetic energy: W_net = KE_final - KE_initial. Positive net work speeds an object up, negative net work slows it down, and zero net work leaves its speed unchanged. The theorem lets you find speeds, forces or stopping distances without using time.
Potential Energy: Potential energy is stored energy that depends on position or configuration. Gravitational potential energy near Earth is PE = m g h, with g = 9.8 m/s^2, where h is measured from a chosen reference level. Only changes in potential energy matter physically. Elastic potential energy in a spring is PE = 1/2 k x^2, where k is the spring constant in N/m and x is the stretch or compression. Because x is squared, doubling the stretch quadruples the stored energy. Lifting an object at constant speed stores energy equal to the work done against gravity.
Conservation of Mechanical Energy: Mechanical energy is the sum of kinetic and potential energy, E = KE + PE. When only conservative forces such as gravity and spring forces do work, total mechanical energy is conserved: KE_i + PE_i = KE_f + PE_f. Energy converts between kinetic and potential forms but the total stays constant. For a freely falling object, v = sqrt(2 g h), independent of mass. When friction or air resistance acts, mechanical energy is not conserved; the missing amount becomes thermal energy, and total energy including heat is still conserved.
Power and Efficiency: Power is the rate of doing work or transferring energy, P = W / t, measured in watts (1 W = 1 J/s). When a constant force acts on an object moving at constant velocity along the force, P = F v. One horsepower is about 746 W, and a kilowatt-hour is an energy unit equal to 3.6 million joules. Efficiency is useful output energy (or power) divided by total input energy (or power), usually given as a percent. Real machines have efficiency below 100 percent because some input energy is wasted, mostly as heat.
